entities.summary:
Adela of Normandy (c. 1067–1137) was a daughter of William the Conqueror and wife of Count Stephen of Blois, making her one of the most politically connected women in early twelfth-century Europe. She was renowned for her intelligence, administrative ability, and political acumen — Orderic Vitalis and other chroniclers described her as far more capable than her husband, whom she famously persuaded to return to the First Crusade after he had fled the siege of Antioch.

Adela exercised effective regency governance of the County of Blois during her husband's absences on crusade and after his death at the Battle of Ramla (1102). Her rule was noted for its justice and competence. More significantly, she was the mother of King Stephen of England — whose reign (1135–1154) produced the devastating civil war known as 'the Anarchy' — and of Theobald IV, Count of Blois.

Her correspondence with Anselm of Canterbury and her intellectual engagement with contemporary theological debates mark her as one of the most educated women of her generation. In later life she entered the Abbey of Marcigny as a Cluniac nun, retiring from political life. She represents the exceptional women of the Norman ruling dynasty who exercised real power in a political world theoretically closed to them, and who shaped European history through both their governance and their progeny.
